claim: TRPV2 plays a critical role in neuronal development, cardiac function, immunity, and cancer.
source: Transient receptor potential vanilloid 2 (TRPV2) plays a critical role in neuronal development, cardiac function, immunity, and cancer.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established roles of TRPV2 in various physiological processes.

claim: Cannabidiol (CBD) is the non-psychotropic therapeutically active ingredient of Cannabis sativa.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), the non-psychotropic therapeutically active ingredient of Cannabis sativa, is an activator of TRPV2 and also modulates other transient receptor potential (TRP) channels.
evidence: This statement describes CBD as a known compound from Cannabis sativa with specific properties.

claim: CBD is an activator of TRPV2.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), the non-psychotropic therapeutically active ingredient of Cannabis sativa, is an activator of TRPV2 and also modulates other transient receptor potential (TRP) channels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Qin et al., 2008) in the introduction.

claim: CBD modulates other transient receptor potential (TRP) channels.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), the non-psychotropic therapeutically active ingredient of Cannabis sativa, is an activator of TRPV2 and also modulates other transient receptor potential (TRP) channels.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction (Qin et al., 2008; De Petrocellis et al., 2012; Smart et al., 2000; De Petrocellis et al., 2008).

claim: Structures of full-length rat TRPV2 channel in apo and CBD-bound states in nanodiscs were determined by cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Here, we determined structures of the full-length rat TRPV2 channel in apo and CBD-bound states in nanodiscs by cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: This is the primary experimental finding of the manuscript, supported by the cryo-EM data presented.

claim: CBD interacts with TRPV2 through a hydrophobic pocket located between S5 and S6 helices of adjacent subunits.
source: We show that CBD interacts with TRPV2 through a hydrophobic pocket located between S5 and S6 helices of adjacent subunits, which differs from known ligand and lipid binding sites in other TRP channels.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing CBD density in this location (Figure 1B, Figure 2).

claim: The CBD binding site in TRPV2 differs from known ligand and lipid binding sites in other TRP channels.
source: We show that CBD interacts with TRPV2 through a hydrophobic pocket located between S5 and S6 helices of adjacent subunits, which differs from known ligand and lipid binding sites in other TRP channels.
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously published TRP channel structures.

claim: The S4-S5 linker plays a critical role in channel gating upon CBD binding.
source: CBD-bound TRPV2 structures revealed that the S4-S5 linker plays a critical role in channel gating upon CBD binding.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparisons between apo and CBD-bound states showing conformational changes in the S4-S5 linker (Figure 3).

claim: Two distinct TRPV2 apo states were visualized in a lipid environment using nanodiscs.
source: Additionally, nanodiscs permitted us to visualize two distinct TRPV2 apo states in a lipid environment.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data showing two different apo structures (TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2APO_2).

claim: Two TRPV2 structures in apo state were resolved to 3.7 Å (TRPV2APO_1) and 4.0 Å (TRPV2APO_2).
source: We now report two TRPV2 structures determined in an apo state resolved to 3.7 Å (TRPV2APO_1) and 4.0 Å (TRPV2APO_2) and two TRPV2 structures determined in the presence of 30 μM CBD resolved to 3.4 Å (TRPV2CBD_1) and 3.2 Å (TRPV2CBD_2) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM data and resolution calculations.

claim: Two TRPV2 structures in the presence of 30 μM CBD were resolved to 3.4 Å (TRPV2CBD_1) and 3.2 Å (TRPV2CBD_2).
source: We now report two TRPV2 structures determined in an apo state resolved to 3.7 Å (TRPV2APO_1) and 4.0 Å (TRPV2APO_2) and two TRPV2 structures determined in the presence of 30 μM CBD resolved to 3.4 Å (TRPV2CBD_1) and 3.2 Å (TRPV2CBD_2) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM data and resolution calculations.

claim: In both TRPV2CBD_1 and TRPV2CBD_2, CBD density occupies the newly proposed CBD-binding site between S5 and S6 helices of adjacent subunits.
source: In both TRPV2CBD_1 and TRPV2CBD_2, CBD density occupies the newly proposed CBD-binding site between S5 and S6 helices of adjacent subunits, but both channels adopt non-conducting conformations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density maps showing CBD in this location (Figure 1B).

claim: Both TRPV2CBD_1 and TRPV2CBD_2 adopt non-conducting conformations.
source: In both TRPV2CBD_1 and TRPV2CBD_2, CBD density occupies the newly proposed CBD-binding site between S5 and S6 helices of adjacent subunits, but both channels adopt non-conducting conformations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on pore radius analysis showing occlusion (Figure 1C-D).

claim: TRPV2CBD_1 is very similar to TRPV2APO_1.
source: While TRPV2CBD_1 is very similar to TRPV2APO_1, TRPV2CBD_2 diverges from the non-conducting TRPV2APO_1 state in nanodiscs, suggesting that we have resolved the channel in CBD-bound pre-open states or desensitized states.
evidence: This is based on structural alignment showing low RMSD (0.4 Å) between these structures.

claim: TRPV2CBD_2 diverges from the non-conducting TRPV2APO_1 state in nanodiscs.
source: While TRPV2CBD_1 is very similar to TRPV2APO_1, TRPV2CBD_2 diverges from the non-conducting TRPV2APO_1 state in nanodiscs, suggesting that we have resolved the channel in CBD-bound pre-open states or desensitized states.
evidence: This is based on structural alignment showing higher RMSD (1.9 Å) between these structures.

claim: TRPV2CBD_1 and TRPV2CBD_2 may represent CBD-bound pre-open states or desensitized states.
source: While TRPV2CBD_1 is very similar to TRPV2APO_1, TRPV2CBD_2 diverges from the non-conducting TRPV2APO_1 state in nanodiscs, suggesting that we have resolved the channel in CBD-bound pre-open states or desensitized states.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural data showing non-conducting conformations with CBD bound.

claim: TRPV2APO_2 is in a partially open conformation.
source: Moreover, nanodiscs allow us to observe TRPV2APO_2 state in a partially open conformation, suggesting that lipids play an important role in channel transitions between closed and open states.
evidence: This is based on pore analysis showing an open selectivity filter (Figure 1C-D).

claim: Lipids play an important role in channel transitions between closed and open states.
source: Moreover, nanodiscs allow us to observe TRPV2APO_2 state in a partially open conformation, suggesting that lipids play an important role in channel transitions between closed and open states.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of different conformations in lipid nanodiscs.

claim: TRPV2 does not contribute to thermal nociception in vivo.
source: Transient receptor potential vanilloid 2 (TRPV2) belongs to the thermoTRPV subfamily of TRP channels (TRPV1-TRPV4), yet TRPV2 does not contribute to thermal nociception in vivo and is insensitive to vanilloids (Park et al., 2011; Perálvarez-Marín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Park et al., 2011; Perálvarez-Marín et al., 2013).

claim: TRPV2 is insensitive to vanilloids.
source: Transient receptor potential vanilloid 2 (TRPV2) belongs to the thermoTRPV subfamily of TRP channels (TRPV1-TRPV4), yet TRPV2 does not contribute to thermal nociception in vivo and is insensitive to vanilloids (Park et al., 2011; Perálvarez-Marín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Park et al., 2011; Perálvarez-Marín et al., 2013).

claim: TRPV2 has been the least studied among TRPV channels due to the lack of specific pharmacological agonists or antagonists.
source: It has been the least studied among TRPV channels due to the lack of specific pharmacological agonists or antagonists (Perálvarez-Marín et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Perálvarez-Marín et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2008).

claim: CBD is a TRPV2 agonist.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), a natural product of the Cannabis sativa plant, is a TRPV2 agonist (Qin et al., 2008) which has been recently used to demonstrate the important role of TRPV2 in the inhibition of glioblastoma multiforme cell proliferation (Perálvarez-Marín et al., 2013; Liberati et al., 2014; Nabissi et al., 2010; Nabissi et al., 2015; Nabissi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Qin et al., 2008).

claim: CBD has been used to demonstrate the important role of TRPV2 in the inhibition of glioblastoma multiforme cell proliferation.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), a natural product of the Cannabis sativa plant, is a TRPV2 agonist (Qin et al., 2008) which has been recently used to demonstrate the important role of TRPV2 in the inhibition of glioblastoma multiforme cell proliferation (Perálvarez-Marín et al., 2013; Liberati et al., 2014; Nabissi et al., 2010; Nabissi et al., 2015; Nabissi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Perálvarez-Marín et al., 2013; Liberati et al., 2014; Nabissi et al., 2010; Nabissi et al., 2015; Nabissi et al., 2013).

claim: TRPV2 is on the list of important anti-tumor drug targets.
source: These findings place TRPV2 on the list of important anti-tumor drug targets (Perálvarez-Marín et al., 2013; Liberati et al., 2014; Nabissi et al., 2010; Nabissi et al., 2015; Nabissi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Perálvarez-Marín et al., 2013; Liberati et al., 2014; Nabissi et al., 2010; Nabissi et al., 2015; Nabissi et al., 2013).

claim: Cannabinoids and cannabinoid analogs have been reported to activate a variety of TRP channels, including TRPV1-4.
source: Cannabinoids and cannabinoid analogs have been reported to activate a variety of TRP channels, including TRPV1-4 (Qin et al., 2008; De Petrocellis et al., 2012; Smart et al., 2000) and TRPA1 (De Petrocellis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Qin et al., 2008; De Petrocellis et al., 2012; Smart et al., 2000).

claim: Cannabinoids and cannabinoid analogs have been reported to activate TRPA1.
source: Cannabinoids and cannabinoid analogs have been reported to activate a variety of TRP channels, including TRPV1-4 (Qin et al., 2008; De Petrocellis et al., 2012; Smart et al., 2000) and TRPA1 (De Petrocellis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (De Petrocellis et al., 2008).

claim: CBD activates TRPV2 with an EC50 of 3.7 µM for rat TRPV2.
source: CBD activates TRPV2 with an EC50 of 3.7 µM for rat TRPV2 (Qin et al., 2008), making it a good candidate for the investigation of TRP channel modulation by CBD using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Qin et al., 2008).

claim: A cannabinoid binding site could be conserved within the TRP channel family.
source: Additionally, the activation of other TRP channels by CBD suggests that a cannabinoid binding site could be conserved within this family of channels (Qin et al., 2008; De Petrocellis et al., 2012; Smart et al., 2000; De Petrocellis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that CBD activates multiple TRP channels.

claim: The TRPV2 channel has been the subject of several cryo-EM studies that offered insights on TRPV2 channel gating.
source: Recently, the TRPV2 channel has been the subject of several cryo-EM studies that offered thought-provoking insights on TRPV2 channel gating (Huynh et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016; Dosey et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Huynh et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016; Dosey et al., 2019).

claim: Studies using the rabbit TRPV2 pore turret deletion mutant concluded that the pore turret region in rabbit TRPV2 is not essential for channel function.
source: Studies using the rabbit TRPV2 pore turret deletion mutant (Zubcevic et al., 2016) and full-length engineered resiniferatoxin (RTx)-sensitive channel (Zubcevic et al., 2019a) concluded that the pore turret region in rabbit TRPV2 is not essential for channel function and that although mostly unresolved, it adopts a conformation perpendicular to the lipid membrane (Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Zubcevic et al., 2016; Zubcevic et al., 2019a).

claim: The pore turret in rabbit TRPV2 adopts a conformation perpendicular to the lipid membrane.
source: Studies using the rabbit TRPV2 pore turret deletion mutant (Zubcevic et al., 2016) and full-length engineered resiniferatoxin (RTx)-sensitive channel (Zubcevic et al., 2019a) concluded that the pore turret region in rabbit TRPV2 is not essential for channel function and that although mostly unresolved, it adopts a conformation perpendicular to the lipid membrane (Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016).

claim: Engineered RTx-sensitive rabbit TRPV2 channel undergoes symmetry transitions when activated by RTx.
source: These studies also suggested that engineered RTx-sensitive rabbit TRPV2 channel undergoes symmetry transitions when activated by RTx (Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016).

claim: Structures using the rat TRPV2 pore turret deletion mutant and full-length channel showed that the pore turret region plays a vital role in rat TRPV2 gating.
source: On the other hand, structures using the rat TRPV2 pore turret deletion mutant (Dosey et al., 2019) and full-length channel (Huynh et al., 2016; Dosey et al., 2019) showed that the pore turret region plays a vital role in rat TRPV2 gating, whether in the presence or in the absences of ligands (Huynh et al., 2016; Dosey et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Huynh et al., 2016; Dosey et al., 2019).

claim: The previous full-length rat TRPV2 structure was determined at ∼5 Å resolution in detergent.
source: The previous full-length rat TRPV2 structure from our group was determined at ∼5 Å resolution in detergent (Huynh et al., 2016), but at this resolution we could not build side chains, accurately assign the functional state of the channel or resolve pore turrets (Huynh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Huynh et al., 2016).

claim: At ∼5 Å resolution, side chains could not be built, the functional state of the channel could not be accurately assigned, and pore turrets could not be resolved.
source: The previous full-length rat TRPV2 structure from our group was determined at ∼5 Å resolution in detergent (Huynh et al., 2016), but at this resolution we could not build side chains, accurately assign the functional state of the channel or resolve pore turrets (Huynh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the authors' prior experience with lower resolution structures.

claim: The pore turret structure in the full-length rat TRPV2 channel in detergent has been resolved and shown to adopt a conformation parallel to the lipid membrane.
source: Recently, the pore turret structure in the full-length rat TRPV2 channel in detergent has been resolved (Dosey et al., 2019) and shown to adopt a conformation parallel to the lipid membrane.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Dosey et al., 2019).

claim: The full-length rat TRPV2 structure in detergent has been assigned to the open state of the channel.
source: Moreover, this full-length rat TRPV2 structure in detergent has been assigned to the open state of the channel (Dosey et al., 2019), however the provided cryo-EM data were not of sufficient quality to independently confirm this proposed channel conformation or the pore turret structure of the channel.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Dosey et al., 2019).

claim: The cryo-EM data from Dosey et al., 2019 were not of sufficient quality to independently confirm the proposed channel conformation or the pore turret structure.
source: Moreover, this full-length rat TRPV2 structure in detergent has been assigned to the open state of the channel (Dosey et al., 2019), however the provided cryo-EM data were not of sufficient quality to independently confirm this proposed channel conformation or the pore turret structure of the channel.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of the quality of prior work.

claim: The TRPV2APO_1 pore is occluded at the selectivity filter (Gly606 and Met607) and the lower gate of the channel (Met645 and His651).
source: The TRPV2APO_1 pore is occluded at the selectivity filter (Gly606 and Met607) and the lower gate of the channel (Met645 and His651), representing a closed TRPV2 state in nanodiscs.
evidence: This is based on pore analysis of the TRPV2APO_1 structure (Figure 1C-D).

claim: TRPV2APO_1 represents a closed TRPV2 state in nanodiscs.
source: The TRPV2APO_1 pore is occluded at the selectivity filter (Gly606 and Met607) and the lower gate of the channel (Met645 and His651), representing a closed TRPV2 state in nanodiscs.
evidence: This is inferred from the pore occlusion observed in the structure.

claim: The TRPV2APO_2 pore selectivity filter is wide open.
source: On the other hand, the TRPV2APO_2 pore selectivity filter is wide open, suggesting that this structure is in a partially open state.
evidence: This is based on pore analysis of the TRPV2APO_2 structure (Figure 1C-D).

claim: TRPV2APO_2 is in a partially open state.
source: On the other hand, the TRPV2APO_2 pore selectivity filter is wide open, suggesting that this structure is in a partially open state.
evidence: This is inferred from the open selectivity filter observed in the structure.

claim: The TRPV2CBD_1 and TRPV2CBD_2 pores are in two different non-conducting states.
source: The TRPV2CBD_1 and TRPV2CBD_2 pores are in two different non-conducting states, suggesting that we may have resolved CBD-bound pre-open or desensitized states of the channel.
evidence: This is based on pore analysis of the CBD-bound structures (Figure 1C-D).

claim: All cryo-EM data obtained for apo and 30 μM CBD-bound TRPV2 reconstituted into nanodiscs was analyzed using RELION 3.0 without symmetry imposition during the initial reconstruction and classification.
source: All cryo-EM data obtained for apo and 30 μM CBD-bound TRPV2 reconstituted into nanodiscs was analyzed using RELION 3.0 without symmetry imposition during the initial reconstruction and classification (Zivanov et al., 2018; Scheres, 2016; Scheres, 2012).
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology used.

claim: After the initial round of 3D classification, the best set of particles from each dataset was evaluated by the Map Symmetry function in PHENIX and assigned four-fold symmetry based on the highest correlation coefficient score.
source: After the initial round of 3D classification, the best set of particles from each dataset was evaluated by the Map Symmetry function in PHENIX (Adams et al., 2002) and assigned four-fold symmetry based on the highest correlation coefficient score (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–4, Table 1).
evidence: This describes the symmetry determination methodology used.

claim: All four newly resolved full-length rat TRPV2 channels form homo-tetramers featuring six transmembrane helices (S1-S6) spanning the transmembrane domain (TMD) with six ankyrin repeat domains (ARDs) splayed out like a pinwheel on the cytoplasmic face of the protein.
source: As in previous cryo-EM structures of TRPV2 (Zubcevic et al., 2016; Huynh et al., 2016; Dosey et al., 2019; Zubcevic et al., 2019a), all four newly resolved full-length rat TRPV2 channels form homo-tetramers featuring six transmembrane helices (S1-S6) spanning the transmembrane domain (TMD) with six ankyrin repeat domains (ARDs) splayed out like a pinwheel on the cytoplasmic face of the protein, with the ARDs of adjacent monomers connected through a β-sheet region composed of the N-linker between the ARDs and the TMD and a portion of the C-terminus.
evidence: This is based on the structural data obtained in this study and comparison with prior structures.

claim: S1-S4 form a bundle, while S5, S6 and the pore helix (PH) extend away from S1-S4 to domain swap with adjacent monomers and form the pore.
source: S1-S4 form a bundle, while S5, S6 and the pore helix (PH) extend away from S1-S4 to domain swap with adjacent monomers and form the pore.
evidence: This is based on the structural data obtained in this study.

claim: All four maps obtained in this study lack fully resolved density for the pore turret between the top of S5 and the pore helix.
source: Despite working with the full-length rat TRPV2 protein, all four maps obtained in this study lack fully resolved density for the pore turret between the top of S5 and the pore helix (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM density maps obtained in this study (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).

claim: Partial density for the pore turret region indicates that the pore turret forms a flexible loop perpendicular to the lipid membrane.
source: Nevertheless, partial density for this region of the channel indicates that the pore turret forms a flexible loop perpendicular to the lipid membrane, which agrees with observations in the full-length engineered RTx-sensitive rabbit TRPV2 channel (Zubcevic et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is based on the partial density observed in the cryo-EM maps and comparison with prior work.

claim: The data do not agree with the observation that the charged and polar flexible pore turret loop is arranged parallel to the plasma membrane as reported for the full-length rat TRPV2 structure in detergent.
source: Thus, our data do not agree with the observation that the charged and polar flexible pore turret loop is arranged parallel to the plasma membrane as it has been reported for the full-length rat TRPV2 structure in detergent (Dosey et al., 2019) (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the current data with prior work (Dosey et al., 2019).

claim: The CBD binding pocket is located between the S5 and S6 helices of adjacent TRPV2 monomers.
source: Comparison between full-length rat TRPV2 in the apo (TRPV2APO_1, TRPV2APO_2) and the CBD-bound (TRPV2CBD_1, TRPV2CBD_2) states in nanodiscs allowed us to identify the CBD-binding pocket, which is located between the S5 and S6 helices of adjacent TRPV2 monomers (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of apo and CBD-bound structures (Figure 1A-B).

claim: The non-protein density assigned to the CBD ligand is not present in the final or half maps of either apo TRPV2 structure.
source: The non-protein density assigned to the CBD ligand is not present in the final or half maps of either apo TRPV2 structure and is present in all half maps of the CBD-bound structures (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density maps (Figure 1—figure supplement 10).

claim: The non-protein density assigned to CBD is present in all half maps of the CBD-bound structures.
source: The non-protein density assigned to the CBD ligand is not present in the final or half maps of either apo TRPV2 structure and is present in all half maps of the CBD-bound structures (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density maps (Figure 1—figure supplement 10).

claim: The density unique to the dataset with added CBD is similar in size and shape to CBD and has been assigned to CBD.
source: Since this density is unique to the dataset with added CBD and is similar in size and shape to CBD, we have assigned it to CBD (Figure 1A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the presence of density only in CBD-bound structures and its shape (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: All full-length rat TRPV2 maps presented in this manuscript have extra non-protein density that could be attributed to lipids.
source: All full-length rat TRPV2 maps presented in this manuscript also have extra non-protein density that could be attributed to lipids (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on observation of non-protein density in the cryo-EM maps (Figure 1A).

claim: Several cryo-EM studies on TRPV channels observed very similar lipid densities in different TMD hydrophobic pockets and proposed that some of these lipids are important for channel function and structure.
source: Several cryo-EM studies on TRPV channels also observed very similar lipid densities in different TMD hydrophobic pockets and proposed that some of these lipids are important for channel function and structure (Gao et al., 2016; Hughes et al., 2018a; McGoldrick et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2018; Zubcevic et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Gao et al., 2016; Hughes et al., 2018a; McGoldrick et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2018; Zubcevic et al., 2018a).

claim: Ligand binding sites in several other TRPV channel cryo-EM structures determined so far have been also occupied by lipids in their apo structures.
source: It is interesting to note that ligand binding sites in several other TRPV channel cryo-EM structures determined so far have been also occupied by lipids in their apo structures (Gao et al., 2016; Hughes et al., 2018a; McGoldrick et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2018; Zubcevic et al., 2018a), which is not the case for the CBD binding pocket determined here (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Gao et al., 2016; Hughes et al., 2018a; McGoldrick et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2018; Zubcevic et al., 2018a).

claim: The CBD binding pocket in TRPV2 is not occupied by lipids in the apo structures.
source: It is interesting to note that ligand binding sites in several other TRPV channel cryo-EM structures determined so far have been also occupied by lipids in their apo structures (Gao et al., 2016; Hughes et al., 2018a; McGoldrick et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2018; Zubcevic et al., 2018a), which is not the case for the CBD binding pocket determined here (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on the absence of lipid density in the CBD binding pocket in apo structures (Figure 1A).

claim: The CBD binding site is lined with mostly hydrophobic and aromatic residues including Leu631, Tyr634, Val635 and Leu638 on the S6 helix of one monomer and Leu537, Phe540, Leu541 on the S5 helix and Met640 on the S6 helix of an adjacent monomer.
source: A comparison of the models built into the TRPV2APO_1, TRPV2CBD_1, and TRPV2CBD_2 cryo-EM maps revealed that the CBD binding site is lined with mostly hydrophobic and aromatic residues. These include Leu631, Tyr634, Val635 and Leu638 on the S6 helix of one monomer and Leu537, Phe540, Leu541 on the S5 helix and Met640 on the S6 helix of an adjacent monomer, while the pore helix of the adjacent monomer caps the pocket with residues Phe601 and Thr604 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the atomic models built into the cryo-EM maps (Figure 2).

claim: The pore helix of the adjacent monomer caps the CBD binding pocket with residues Phe601 and Thr604.
source: A comparison of the models built into the TRPV2APO_1, TRPV2CBD_1, and TRPV2CBD_2 cryo-EM maps revealed that the CBD binding site is lined with mostly hydrophobic and aromatic residues. These include Leu631, Tyr634, Val635 and Leu638 on the S6 helix of one monomer and Leu537, Phe540, Leu541 on the S5 helix and Met640 on the S6 helix of an adjacent monomer, while the pore helix of the adjacent monomer caps the pocket with residues Phe601 and Thr604 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the atomic models built into the cryo-EM maps (Figure 2).

claim: CBD is composed of a cyclohexene headgroup with small hydrophobic substitutions, a middle aromatic ring with two free phenolic hydroxyl groups, and a 5-carbon acyl tail.
source: CBD is composed of a cyclohexene headgroup with small hydrophobic substitutions, a middle aromatic ring with two free phenolic hydroxyl groups, and a 5-carbon acyl tail (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the known chemical structure of CBD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: The hydrophobic head group of CBD enters furthest into the CBD-binding pocket, where it is surrounded by aromatic and hydrophobic residues.
source: The hydrophobic head group enters furthest into the CBD-binding pocket, where it is surrounded by aromatic and hydrophobic residues.
evidence: This is based on the position of CBD in the binding pocket observed in the structures.

claim: Tyr634 rotates between TRPV2APO_1 and the CBD-bound structures to sit next to CBD.
source: Notably, although most of the residues in this pocket are in similar positions in all three structures, Tyr634 rotates between TRPV2APO_1 and the CBD-bound structures (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) to sit next to CBD, which may be due to the hydrophobic effect shielding CBD from ions in the pore.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structures (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: The rotation of Tyr634 may be due to the hydrophobic effect shielding CBD from ions in the pore.
source: Notably, although most of the residues in this pocket are in similar positions in all three structures, Tyr634 rotates between TRPV2APO_1 and the CBD-bound structures (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) to sit next to CBD, which may be due to the hydrophobic effect shielding CBD from ions in the pore.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural observation.

claim: The two free phenolic hydroxyl groups of the middle region of CBD fit between turns of the α-helices on either side, potentially coordinating via bifurcated hydrogen bonds with the carbonyl of Leu631 and amide of Tyr634 on S6 of one monomer and the carbonyl of Leu537 and the amide of Leu541 on S5 of the adjacent monomer.
source: The two free phenolic hydroxyl groups of the middle region of CBD fit between turns of the α-helices on either side, potentially coordinating via bifurcated hydrogen bonds with the carbonyl of Leu631 and amide of Tyr634 on S6 of one monomer and the carbonyl of Leu537 and the amide of Leu541 on S5 of the adjacent monomer (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on the position of CBD and distances measured in the structures (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: The Leu537 sidechain has rotated in the CBD-bound structures to accommodate the aromatic ring of CBD.
source: Additionally, the Leu537 sidechain has rotated in the CBD-bound structures to accommodate the aromatic ring of CBD (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of apo and CBD-bound structures (Figure 2).

claim: Density for the CBD acyl tail trails off, indicating flexibility where the acyl tail meets lipids in the lipid bilayer.
source: Density for the CBD acyl tail trails off (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating flexibility where the acyl tail meets lipids in the lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is based on the quality of density for the acyl tail region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: CBD was oriented with the headgroup on the interior of the pocket and the tail extending into the lipid bilayer because the ligand density on the interior of the pocket was a poor fit for a linear acyl tail and this configuration did not stay stably in the density during PHENIX refinements.
source: CBD was oriented with the headgroup on the interior of the pocket and the tail extending into the lipid bilayer because the ligand density on the interior of the pocket was a poor fit for a linear acyl tail and this configuration did not stay stably in the density during PHENIX refinements.
evidence: This is based on model building and refinement procedures.

claim: An alternate pose of CBD rotated 180° around its longest axis was tested but clashed with the Leu537 sidechain in the TRPV2CBD_1 structure.
source: An alternate pose of the ligand was also tested, with CBD rotated 180° around its longest axis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), turning the headgroup over in the interior of the pocket. While this pose was stable in the ligand density during refinement, it clashed with the Leu537 sidechain in the TRPV2CBD_1 structure, indicating the original pose as the optimal fit for this data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on testing alternative CBD orientations during model building (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Mutating some of the smaller hydrophobic residues in the CBD binding pocket to a bulky aromatic residue like phenylalanine could alter CBD access to the pocket.
source: Based on the CBD binding site identified in out cryo-EM maps, we predicted that mutating some of the smaller hydrophobic residues in this pocket to a bulky aromatic residue like phenylalanine could alter CBD access to the pocket (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the structural data.

claim: Many of the residues on the interior of the binding pocket are bulky aromatic groups and are highly conserved across thermoTRPV channels.
source: Many of the residues on the interior of the binding pocket, which make contacts with the hydrophobic head group are already bulky aromatic groups and are additionally highly conserved across thermoTRPV channels, possibly indicating a crucial role at the tetramerization interface (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), so we focused on mutating Leu541, Leu631, and Val635 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).

claim: The conservation of bulky aromatic residues in the CBD binding pocket possibly indicates a crucial role at the tetramerization interface.
source: Many of the residues on the interior of the binding pocket, which make contacts with the hydrophobic head group are already bulky aromatic groups and are additionally highly conserved across thermoTRPV channels, possibly indicating a crucial role at the tetramerization interface (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), so we focused on mutating Leu541, Leu631, and Val635 (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the conservation pattern.

claim: The ratio of currents induced by 20 μM CBD and 100 μM 2-APB was higher in cells transfected with the Leu541Phe-Leu631Phe mutant compared to wild type TRPV2.
source: Whole cell patch clamp recordings showed that the ratio of currents induced by 20 μM CBD and 100 μM 2-APB was higher in cells transfected with the Leu541Phe-Leu631Phe mutant compared to wild type TRPV2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).

claim: Neither 20 μM CBD nor 100 μM 2-APB induced any current in non-transfected cells.
source: Neither 20 μM CBD nor 100 μM 2-APB induced any current in non-transfected cells and in cells transfected with the Val635Phe mutant, indicating that the latter mutant was non-functional (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The Val635Phe mutant was non-functional.
source: Neither 20 μM CBD nor 100 μM 2-APB induced any current in non-transfected cells and in cells transfected with the Val635Phe mutant, indicating that the latter mutant was non-functional (data not shown).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of current in cells transfected with this mutant.

claim: Residues Leu541 and Leu631 may be involved in CBD modulation of the channel.
source: These electrophysiological results suggest that residues Leu541 and Leu631 may be involved in CBD modulation of the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the altered CBD/2-APB current ratio in the double mutant.

claim: The alignment of TRPV2APO_1 with TRPV2CBD_1 based on the tetrameric pore had an R.M.S.D. of 0.4 Å.
source: The alignment of these three structures based on the tetrameric pore (between residues Asp536-His651) had a low root mean square deviation (R.M.S.D.): 0.4 Å for TRPV2APO_1 to TRPV2CBD_1, and 0.5 Å for TRPV2APO_1 to TRPV2CBD_2.
evidence: This is based on structural alignment calculations.

claim: The alignment of TRPV2APO_1 with TRPV2CBD_2 based on the tetrameric pore had an R.M.S.D. of 0.5 Å.
source: The alignment of these three structures based on the tetrameric pore (between residues Asp536-His651) had a low root mean square deviation (R.M.S.D.): 0.4 Å for TRPV2APO_1 to TRPV2CBD_1, and 0.5 Å for TRPV2APO_1 to TRPV2CBD_2.
evidence: This is based on structural alignment calculations.

claim: The global alignment of TRPV2APO_1 with TRPV2CBD_1 had an R.M.S.D. of 0.6 Å.
source: While the global alignment of the TRPV2APO_1 with TRPV2CBD_1 had an R.M.S.D. of 0.6 Å, the global alignment of TRPV2APO_1 with TRPV2CBD_2 had a higher R.M.S.D. of 1.9 Å.
evidence: This is based on structural alignment calculations.

claim: The global alignment of TRPV2APO_1 with TRPV2CBD_2 had an R.M.S.D. of 1.9 Å.
source: While the global alignment of the TRPV2APO_1 with TRPV2CBD_1 had an R.M.S.D. of 0.6 Å, the global alignment of TRPV2APO_1 with TRPV2CBD_2 had a higher R.M.S.D. of 1.9 Å.
evidence: This is based on structural alignment calculations.

claim: TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2CBD_1 are essentially identical structures based on tetrameric pore alignment.
source: Based on the tetrameric pore alignment, TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2CBD_1 are essentially identical structures (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the low RMSD and visual comparison (Figure 3A-C).

claim: The cryo-EM map quality for TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2CBD_1 allowed resolution of the distal C-terminus up to residue Leu719.
source: The cryo-EM map quality for these structures allowed us to resolve the distal C-terminus for both of these structures up to residue Leu719 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is based on the quality of the cryo-EM density maps (Figure 3—figure supplements 2-3).

claim: The distal C-terminus in TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2CBD_1 formed a short helix that interacts with the N-terminal β-sheet region and ARD of the adjacent subunit of the channel.
source: The distal C-terminus formed a short helix that interacts with the N-terminal β-sheet region and ARD of the adjacent subunit of the channel (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model built into the cryo-EM density (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: In TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2CBD_1, Trp715 forms CH-π interactions with Pro337, found in the N-linker β-sheet region.
source: For both these structures, Trp715 forms CH-π interactions with Pro337, found in the N-linker β-sheet region, while Glu716 forms polar interactions with Asn263, found in AR5 of the adjacent subunit of the channel (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model and distance measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: In TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2CBD_1, Glu716 forms polar interactions with Asn263, found in AR5 of the adjacent subunit of the channel.
source: For both these structures, Trp715 forms CH-π interactions with Pro337, found in the N-linker β-sheet region, while Glu716 forms polar interactions with Asn263, found in AR5 of the adjacent subunit of the channel (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model and distance measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: In TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2CBD_1, a distal N-terminus was resolved that can be fit to residues Gln30-Asn45 and makes contacts between the ARDs of one monomer and the β-sheet region of the adjacent monomer.
source: Moreover, in both of these structures we resolved a distal N-terminus that can be fit to residues Gln30-Asn45 and which makes contacts between the ARDs of one monomer and the β-sheet region of the adjacent monomer (Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM density and atomic model (Figure 3—figure supplements 2-3).

claim: In TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2CBD_1, Met35 lies in a hydrophobic and aromatic pocket formed by the loops between AR3, AR4 and AR5 and the β-sheet region of an adjacent monomer and makes contacts with Trp333.
source: Met35 lies in a hydrophobic and aromatic pocket formed by the loops between AR3, AR4 and AR5 and the β-sheet region of an adjacent monomer and makes contacts with Trp333.
evidence: This is based on the atomic model (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: In TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2CBD_1, Phe39 sits in a hydrophobic pocket formed by Phe330, Leu 342, Leu 689 and Val681 in the β-sheet region of the adjacent monomer.
source: Phe39 sits in a hydrophobic pocket formed by Phe330, Leu 342, Leu 689 and Val681 in the β-sheet region of the adjacent monomer.
evidence: This is based on the atomic model (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: In TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2CBD_1, Lys123 forms a salt bridge with Glu36 and Lys118 interacts with the backbone carbonyl of Met35.
source: Lys123 forms as salt bridge with Glu36 and Lys118 interacts with the backbone carbonyl of Met35 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model and distance measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: The difference between TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2CBD_1 is a minor shift occurring at the S4-S5 linker, which is likely necessary to accommodate the adjacent CBD molecule.
source: The difference between these two structures is a minor shift occurring at the S4-S5 linker, which is likely necessary to accommodate the adjacent CBD molecule, so TRPV2CBD_1 remains in a CBD-bound but non-conductive state (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison (Figure 3A-B).

claim: TRPV2CBD_1 remains in a CBD-bound but non-conductive state.
source: The difference between these two structures is a minor shift occurring at the S4-S5 linker, which is likely necessary to accommodate the adjacent CBD molecule, so TRPV2CBD_1 remains in a CBD-bound but non-conductive state (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is based on pore analysis showing occlusion.

claim: The R.M.S.D. is 1.8 Å when the two apo TRPV2 structures are aligned based on the tetrameric pore of the channel.
source: In contrast to TRPV2APO_1, TRPV2CBD_1, and TRPV2CBD_2, TRPV2APO_2 adopted a very different conformation in the lipid environment (Figure 1 and Figure 4). The R.M.S.D. is 1.8 Å when the two apo TRPV2 structures are aligned based on the tetrameric pore of the channel (residues Asp536-His651, covering S5-PH-S6).
evidence: This is based on structural alignment calculations.

claim: The most notable difference between TRPV2APO_1 and TRPV2APO_2 is the opening of the selectivity filter.
source: The most notable difference between these two apo states is the opening of the selectivity filter (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is based on pore analysis (Figure 1C-D).

claim: At the TRPV2APO_2 selectivity filter, Met607 has rotated away from the pore.
source: At the TRPV2APO_2 selectivity filter, Met607 has rotated away from the pore (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and the carbonyl of Gly606 has shifted away from the pore by 5 Å (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: The carbonyl of Gly606 has shifted away from the pore by 5 Å in TRPV2APO_2.
source: At the TRPV2APO_2 selectivity filter, Met607 has rotated away from the pore (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and the carbonyl of Gly606 has shifted away from the pore by 5 Å (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on distance measurements in the structures (Figure 4B).

claim: Half of the 5 Å shift of Gly606 can be attributed to the outward shift of the whole pore helix, the other half to an additional shift of the loop between the pore helix and S6.
source: Half of this distance can be attributed to the outward shift of the whole pore helix, the other half to an additional shift of the loop between the pore helix and S6 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis (Figure 4B).

claim: In TRPV2APO_2, Glu609 rotates towards the pore, potentially providing a point of interaction with ions passing through the pore.
source: While both Met607 and Gly606 shift away from the pore, Glu609 rotates towards the pore, potentially providing a point of interaction with ions passing through the pore (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and speculative interpretation (Figure 4A-B).

claim: In TRPV2APO_2, the S5-PH-S6 region of each monomer rotates counterclockwise by 8° independently when viewed from the top.
source: In TRPV2APO_2, the S5-PH-S6 region of each monomer rotates counterclockwise by 8° independently when viewed from the top (Figure 4C) and also moves subtly away from the central axis of the pore, with the pore helix showing an overall movement of 2.3 Å (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and measurements (Figure 4C).

claim: In TRPV2APO_2, the pore helix shows an overall movement of 2.3 Å away from the central axis of the pore.
source: In TRPV2APO_2, the S5-PH-S6 region of each monomer rotates counterclockwise by 8° independently when viewed from the top (Figure 4C) and also moves subtly away from the central axis of the pore, with the pore helix showing an overall movement of 2.3 Å (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and measurements (Figure 4B).

claim: In TRPV2APO_2, the His651 residues at the bottom of the pore keep the helices together.
source: Despite the rotation of the S5-PH-S6 region, the His651 residues at the bottom of the pore keep the helices together and the interplay between the rotation and the anchoring at His651 causes the base of the S6 helix to curve slightly (Figure 4D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis (Figure 4D).

claim: The interplay between the rotation and the anchoring at His651 causes the base of the S6 helix to curve slightly in TRPV2APO_2.
source: Despite the rotation of the S5-PH-S6 region, the His651 residues at the bottom of the pore keep the helices together and the interplay between the rotation and the anchoring at His651 causes the base of the S6 helix to curve slightly (Figure 4D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis (Figure 4D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Although the placement of His651 keeps the pore in a non-conducting state in TRPV2APO_2, the movement of His651 out of the pore could result in a completely open channel.
source: Although this placement of His651 keeps the pore in a non-conducting state, it is easy to imagine that the movement of His651 out of the pore could result in a completely open channel.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural data.

claim: In TRPV2APO_2, the S4-S5 linker rotates by 12° to accommodate the rotation of the S5-PH-S6 region.
source: The rotations of the pore region of TRPV2APO_2 are transmitted to the ARDs through rotation of the S4-S5 linker and the TRP helix. The S4-S5 linker rotates by 12° to accommodate the rotation of the S5-PH-S6 region (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and measurements (Figure 4D).

claim: In TRPV2APO_2, the rotation of the S4-S5 linker is coupled to the TRP helix and ARD rotation of 7° and 8°, respectively.
source: The rotation of the S4-S5 linker is coupled to the TRP helix and ARD rotation of 7° and 8°, respectively (Figure 4C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and measurements (Figure 4C-D).

claim: The flexibility of the loop between the S4-S5 linker and S5 likely contributes to the transformation of individual rotation at the pore monomers to an overall rotation of the whole cytoplasmic face of the channel.
source: The flexibility of the loop between the S4-S5 linker and S5 likely contributes to the transformation of individual rotation at the pore monomers to an overall rotation of the whole cytoplasmic face of the channel.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural observations.

claim: The newly obtained cryo-EM results are consistent with previous observations that the purified full-length rat TRPV2 channel displays activity in the presence of ligand as well as exhibiting long spontaneous opening events in the absence of ligands when reconstituted into artificial liposomes.
source: Our newly obtained cryo-EM results are consistent with the previous observations that the purified full-length rat TRPV2 channel displays activity in the presence of ligand as well as exhibiting long spontaneous opening events in the absence of ligands when reconstituted into artificial liposomes (Huynh et al., 2016; Huynh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior electrophysiology studies (Huynh et al., 2016; Huynh et al., 2014).

claim: The membrane environment permits channel transitions between closed and open states without the addition of specific activators.
source: Based on these electrophysiological studies and the conformational changes resolved in TRPV2APO_2, we could speculate that the membrane environment permits channel transitions between closed and open states without the addition of specific activators.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural data and prior electrophysiology.

claim: Nanodisc technology allowed resolution of four different full-length rat TRPV2 structures in lipid membranes and observation of membrane lipids that associated with the channel.
source: Here, we have presented apo and CBD-bound full-length rat TRPV2 structures in a near native lipid environment. Nanodisc technology allowed us to resolve four different full-length rat TRPV2 structures in lipid membranes and observe membrane lipids that associated with the channel.
evidence: This is based on the experimental approach and results obtained.

claim: The novel CBD binding site in the TRPV2 channel was identified.
source: We were able to identify the novel CBD binding site in the TRPV2 channel, which does not correspond to any lipid binding sites in TRPV channels, and determine conformational changes in TRPV2 upon CBD binding.
evidence: This is based on the structural data comparing apo and CBD-bound states.

claim: Conformational changes in TRPV2 upon CBD binding were determined.
source: We were able to identify the novel CBD binding site in the TRPV2 channel, which does not correspond to any lipid binding sites in TRPV channels, and determine conformational changes in TRPV2 upon CBD binding.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison between apo and CBD-bound states.

claim: TRPV channels share ~40% sequence homology.
source: TRPV channels share ~40% sequence homology (Madej and Ziegler, 2018) and thermoTRPV channels (TRPV1-TRPV4) have all been shown to have varying levels of modulation by CBD (Qin et al., 2008; De Petrocellis et al., 2012; Smart et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Madej and Ziegler, 2018).

claim: ThermoTRPV channels (TRPV1-TRPV4) have all been shown to have varying levels of modulation by CBD.
source: TRPV channels share ~40% sequence homology (Madej and Ziegler, 2018) and thermoTRPV channels (TRPV1-TRPV4) have all been shown to have varying levels of modulation by CBD (Qin et al., 2008; De Petrocellis et al., 2012; Smart et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Qin et al., 2008; De Petrocellis et al., 2012; Smart et al., 2000).

claim: The CBD binding site in TRPV2 is highly conserved among TRPV channels.
source: TRPV2 interacts with CBD through a hydrophobic pocket located between S5 and S6 helices of adjacent subunits, which is highly conserved among TRPV channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).

claim: The CBD binding site coincides with the location of the π-helix on S6 in all truncated rat TRPV1 structures in nanodiscs.
source: This binding site coincides with the location of the π-helix on S6 in all truncated rat TRPV1 structures in nanodiscs (Gao et al., 2016), while all the TRPV2 structures reported here had standard α-helixes in this portion of S6.
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior TRPV1 structures (Gao et al., 2016).

claim: All the TRPV2 structures reported here had standard α-helixes in the S6 region where TRPV1 has a π-helix.
source: This binding site coincides with the location of the π-helix on S6 in all truncated rat TRPV1 structures in nanodiscs (Gao et al., 2016), while all the TRPV2 structures reported here had standard α-helixes in this portion of S6.
evidence: This is based on the structural data obtained in this study.

claim: Previous structures of rabbit TRPV2 and frog TRPV4 had standard α-helical S6 helices.
source: Previous structures of rabbit TRPV2 (Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016) and frog TRPV4 (Deng et al., 2018) also had standard α-helical S6 helices.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016; Deng et al., 2018).

claim: TRPV3 studies proposed that a transition between an α-helix and a π-helix on S6 is critical for channel opening.
source: In contrast, TRPV3 studies proposed that a transition between an α-helix and a π-helix on S6 is critical for channel opening (Singh et al., 2018; Zubcevic et al., 2018a; Zubcevic et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Singh et al., 2018; Zubcevic et al., 2018a; Zubcevic et al., 2019b).

claim: It is unclear whether the presence of the π-helix in TRPV1 and TRPV3 channels would hinder or aid CBD binding to the channel.
source: Based on our current results, it is unclear whether the presence of the π-helix in TRPV1 and TRPV3 channels would hinder or aid CBD binding to the channel.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty based on the current structural data.

claim: Studies on the truncated and full-length engineered RTx-sensitive rabbit TRPV2 channel suggested that upon RTx binding TRPV2 undergoes a transition between two-fold and four-fold symmetry.
source: Studies on the truncated (Zubcevic et al., 2018b) and full-length engineered RTx-sensitive rabbit TRPV2 channel (Zubcevic et al., 2019a) suggested that upon RTx binding TRPV2 undergoes a transition between two-fold and four-fold symmetry and that this transition is seen for structures in both amphipols and nanodiscs (Zubcevic et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Zubcevic et al., 2018b; Zubcevic et al., 2019a).

claim: No evidence of two-fold symmetry transition was seen in either of the full-length rat TRPV2 in nanodiscs data sets at any stage of data processing.
source: However, we did not see any evidence of two-fold symmetry transition in either of our full-length rat TRPV2 in nanodiscs data sets at any stage of data processing.
evidence: This is based on the data processing and analysis performed in this study.

claim: There was no indication in the structures that the pore turrets are arranging parallel to the membrane and interact with the lipids in the membrane.
source: Additionally, we did not see any indication in our structures that the pore turrets are arranging parallel to the membrane and interact with the lipids in the membrane (Dosey et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on the structural data obtained in this study and comparison with prior work (Dosey et al., 2019).

claim: In all structures, partial density for the pore turrets was seen extending perpendicularly away from the membrane, confirming similar observations in the full-length engineered RTx-sensitive rabbit TRPV2 channel.
source: Instead, in all of our structures we saw partial density for the pore turrets extending perpendicularly away from the membrane, confirming similar observations in the full-length engineered RTx-sensitive rabbit TRPV2 channel (Zubcevic et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is based on the structural data obtained in this study and comparison with prior work (Zubcevic et al., 2019a).

claim: It seems logical to suggest that structural changes would originate at the S4-S5 linker, which is the closest divergent region to the site of CBD binding.
source: As all of these full-length rat TRPV2 structures are in static states, the forces and timing of the structural changes we observed are unclear. However, it seems logical to suggest that these changes would originate at the S4-S5 linker, which is the closest divergent region to the site of CBD binding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural data.

claim: The S4-S5 linker has previously been suggested to function as the gearbox in TRP channels generally, mediating the transmission of forces between the pore and the rest of the channel.
source: This region has previously been suggested to function as the gearbox in TRP channels generally (Hofmann et al., 2017), mediating the transmission of forces between the pore and the rest of the channel, which is consistent with our observations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Hofmann et al., 2017).

claim: The observations are consistent with recent work on the engineered RTx-sensitive rabbit TRPV2 channel, which showed similar transitions in the S4-S5 linker upon RTx binding.
source: This is also consistent with the recent work on the engineered RTx-sensitive rabbit TRPV2 channel (Zubcevic et al., 2019a), which showed similar transitions in the S4-S5 linker upon RTx binding (Zubcevic et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Zubcevic et al., 2019a).

claim: Previous work has suggested that TRPV2 has some level of constitutive activity.
source: Previous work from our group (Huynh et al., 2016) and others (Penna et al., 2006) has suggested that TRPV2 has some level of constitutive activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Huynh et al., 2016; Penna et al., 2006).

claim: The TRPV2APO_2 structure supports the idea that TRPV2 has some level of constitutive activity.
source: This is supported by the second structure obtained from the apo TRPV2 dataset, TRPV2APO_2.
evidence: This is based on the structural data showing a partially open conformation in the absence of ligand.

claim: TRPV2APO_2 may be a snapshot of a semi-open state of the full-length rat TRPV2 channel.
source: This state may be a snapshot of a semi-open state of the full-length rat TRPV2 channel.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural data.

claim: His651 is not conserved, and the human TRPV2 channel has a serine rather than a histidine in this position.
source: Despite the prominent role His651 seems to be playing in rat TRPV2 structures, it should be noted that His651 is not conserved, and in fact the human TRPV2 channel has a serine rather than a histidine in this position (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).

claim: Similar selectivity filter conformation has been observed in the truncated rat TRPV1 channel upon RTx and double-knot toxin (DkTx) application.
source: Similar selectivity filter conformation has been observed in the truncated rat TRPV1 (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016) channel upon RTx and double-knot toxin (DkTx) application (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and it has been proposed that the selectivity filter plays a critical role in TRPV1 channel gating.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016).

claim: It has been proposed that the selectivity filter plays a critical role in TRPV1 channel gating.
source: Similar selectivity filter conformation has been observed in the truncated rat TRPV1 (Cao et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016) channel upon RTx and double-knot toxin (DkTx) application (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and it has been proposed that the selectivity filter plays a critical role in TRPV1 channel gating.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: All recent TRPV2 cryo-EM studies have made very similar conclusions, suggesting that TRPV1 and TRPV2 share similar gating mechanisms.
source: All recent TRPV2 cryo-EM studies have made very similar conclusions, suggesting that TRPV1 and TRPV2 share similar gating mechanisms (Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Zubcevic et al., 2019a; Zubcevic et al., 2016).

claim: The data support the idea that TRPV1 and TRPV2 share similar gating mechanisms and that the selectivity filter in TRPV2 is important for channel gating.
source: The data presented here support this idea and we conclude that the selectivity filter in TRPV2 is important for channel gating.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data and comparison with prior work.

claim: It has been observed that the distal C-terminus in TRPV1-TRPV3 cryo-EM structures can adopt helical or coil conformations.
source: Recently, it has also been observed that the distal C-terminus in TRPV1-TRPV3 cryo-EM structures can adopt helical or coil conformations (Zubcevic et al., 2019b), which may be associated with TRPV channel gating.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Zubcevic et al., 2019b).

claim: The distal C-terminus conformations may be associated with TRPV channel gating.
source: Recently, it has also been observed that the distal C-terminus in TRPV1-TRPV3 cryo-EM structures can adopt helical or coil conformations (Zubcevic et al., 2019b), which may be associated with TRPV channel gating.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation from prior work (Zubcevic et al., 2019b).

claim: Three of the structures (TRPV2APO_1, TRPV2APO_2, and TRPV2CBD_1) have a helical distal C-terminus, but in TRPV2CBD_2 the distal C-terminus adopts a coil conformation.
source: Three of our structures (TRPV2APO_1, TRPV2APO_2, and TRPV2CBD_1) have a helical distal C-terminus, but in TRPV2CBD_2 the distal C-terminus adopts a coil conformation.
evidence: This is based on the structural data obtained in this study.
